title: Guitar duet with Rappolo on the NORK Gennett session
summary: He recalls the Indianapolis recording where he and Rappolo played guitar duets, Carol Pierce's Marguerite, and that the duet was never released.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Well, Dick Allen was telling me that you once played some guitar duets with rap. Did he play the guitar duets?
Yeah, when we made that recording in Indianapolis, at the time, you know, with the big band, that you played some guitar duets with rap.

Yeah, when we made that recording in Indianapolis, at the time, you know, with the big band, that we, with New Orleans, Harlem Kings, we, rap and I played a duet with two guitars. He played the blues and I made the accompaniments, you know, behind him. But we made the recording, but I never heard anything of it. Did he play much? No, I never heard nothing of it. Did he play much? In fact, Carol Pierce, some of the musicians says they heard it, but I never did hear. Carol Pierce, I heard a piano, because we had three piano players when we went there. Carol Pierce made, he was a pianist, and he, from Strangton, he came from Strangton. And he made a number there, composed a number there by the name of Marguerite. Now, I made that number, but for, I mean, up until this, till this day, I never heard it. I've never heard it. Yeah, that's our record. Yeah, we have it. You got a record on it? Yeah.
Oh, no. Yeah. The guitar never came out though. Maybe it was a test record. You got Marguerite? Yeah. Yeah. Well, that goes to show it. A lot of people have that. Not a lot, but a few.
Yeah, I heard a couple of them tell me that they heard it.
If you want to hear it, you can come up and we'll dig all those things out up at Tulane, I'll show you. Some of the different stuff you got, or I can bring it down here, whatever you want.

Well, I swear, can you imagine a thing like that? And since I recorded that number, I heard all the rest of the numbers, but that one-size number I recorded. Yeah, I heard the record. Now, I heard the numbers of what we made with Jell-Ole Morton, because Jell-Ole Morton sat down and played his, you know, his compositions of Jell-Ole, and Saab and Blues, and some of that. Some of that are two or three numbers. I don't know who it was. But our real piano player at that time was Fritzl, Mike Fritzl, not Mike Fritzl. Mel Stitzel. Mel Stitzel. Mel Stitzel. I'm even getting mixed up with Mike Fritzl. Well, that's almost the same name. Yeah. Okay, he was the owner of the nightclub.
So how did rap play guitar? Did he ever play very much on it? I never really played.

No, just to specialize on blues, that's all. And just one string at the time. He didn't know no chords or nothing, but he just made a practice of that, you know. That's why I had to make the accompaniments on the guitar for what it was. Filled in the chords. But it was really nice. It was really nice. And I don't know for what reason, unless that we might have probably put in something there. Because you see, they only allow you so many measures of so on certain number. And if you go over that, because they can, after you, I believe it's after four measures, or eight measures of a number, like that, they consume you.
Oh yeah, if the melodies are saying that, yeah.
Now that's the only thing that I can see that, because the number was nice. It really, because we practiced on it, you know. But it never had come out.
